According to the Defender of Rights 2020 report, biased data can contribute to algorithmic discrimination when the data used to train algorithms reflects historical biases or lacks representativity, leading to incorrect assumptions about certain groups. For example, if an algorithm is trained on employment data where women are underrepresented and occupy lower positions, it may deduce that women are less productive, thereby reproducing and exacerbating existing biases in recruitment processes.

Similarly, apparently neutral criteria can also lead to discriminatory effects. The report highlights that using seemingly neutral criteria, such as the institution of origin in university algorithms, can indirectly discriminate against certain groups, like youths of foreign origin, due to underlying residential and educational segregation. This demonstrates that even criteria that do not explicitly include prohibited grounds for discrimination can still result in biased outcomes when correlated with other factors.
